subject: biology
title: Sperm Meets Egg
welcome_lead: Watch two specialised cells meet to form the very first cell of a new person.
meta_desc: KS3 Biology adventure on fertilisation and gestation outline.
final_note: You can now describe fertilisation and the rough timeline of human gestation.

concepts.def: Small male sex cell with a tail.
Large female sex cell with food store.
Sperm and egg fuse into one cell.
Ball of dividing cells in the uterus.
Time the baby grows in the uterus.

walkthroughs.body_html: The sperm is small with a tail to swim. The egg is much larger with food stored inside. Each carries half a set of chromosomes.
Inside the oviduct, one sperm joins with the egg. The two nuclei combine. The new cell is a zygote with a full set of chromosomes.
The zygote divides into an embryo which implants in the uterus wall. It grows for about 40 weeks until birth.

mcqs.q: Why does the left ventricle have a thicker muscular wall than the right?
options: The left ventricle is thicker because it handles oxygenated blood, which is harder to pump.
The left ventricle is thicker because it is on the same side as the brain.
It must pump blood at high pressure around the whole body; the right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs.

options: Frameshift mutations are usually silent because cells can correct them.

They are carried in the bloodstream and act on cells with specific receptors for that hormone.
Hormones are released directly into target organs by being injected by glands.

mcqs.q: Why are frameshift mutations usually more severe than point substitutions?
options: Frameshift mutations are usually silent because cells can correct them.
Frameshifts only change the codon at the site of the mutation, like a substitution.
Hormones are released directly into target organs by being injected by glands.
Insertions/deletions of a non-multiple of 3 shift the reading frame, changing every codon downstream of the mutation.
